newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt urges accleration of tough German reforms.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt urges accleration of tough German reforms.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Friday the government would launch a series of reform initiatives next year aimed at making Germany more attractive for corporate investment and curbing unemployment.

The minister outlined a 10-point action plan that includes measures to promote service industries and global trade efforts, as well as to create more venture capital for new entrepreneurs and to further social welfare reforms.

Although the economy is growing again, he said the number of Germans out of work is set to rise to new records in the coming months and only a long-term, painful process of structural reforms could set the stage to create new jobs.

"The economy has started rolling again. But at the same time employment levels are falling further and there is great concern that this winter unemployment will significantly overstep the four million mark," Rexrodt told reporters.
Rexrodt repeated the government's prediction that the German economy would grow around 1.5 percent this year and 2.5 percent next year.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition government is set to decide next month on the details of a broad reform of the income tax system aimed at lowering tax rates beginning in 1999 and creating a net tax cut of some 30 billion marks ($19.27 billion).

Speaking in Bonn about the implementation of budget and regulatory reforms, Rexrodt cited examples of progress such as the partial privatisation of phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG and a new law allowing a reduction in sick pay.

But Rexrodt sharply criticised trade unions for blocking further reforms and slammed employers for failing to stand up to the unions and use the leeway to cut sick pay to 80 percent of wages and instead agreeing to maintain the status quo.
"Now the state cannot be made to blame again for this utter failure," he said. "Everyone involved -- the state, business and labour -- must direct their actions towards the goal of creating jobs."

In order to step up the pace of reform, Rexrodt said he would launch two initiatives next year, one aimed at promoting service industries and another to privatise state services such as airports and road construction.

But despite progress the government has made over the past year, criticism of the slowness of change is growing louder and industry is increasingly moving production abroad to take advantage of lower costs in neighbouring countries.

"A start has been made toward improving Germany as a production centre, but the pace of reform is still too slow to overcome weak investment and the unemployment crisis," the economic daily Handelsblatt wrote in an editorial on Friday.

The government announced this week it plans to cut the solidarity tax -- a surcharge on income tax bills to finance German unification -- two points to 5.5 percent and to cut some corporate taxes in 1998.

At the same time, Kohl's centre-right coalition announced plans for a new tax on energy consumption and opposition politicians and economists suggested this could backfire and result in a sharp rise in value added tax.
Rolf Peffekoven, an independent economist, told German television that he thought value added tax could rise to as much as 17 percent from the current rate of 15 percent.
